summary:
Sort; for each fixed first value, squeeze the other two from both ends of the rest: below the target, move the
low pointer up; above, move the high pointer down. Track the sum with the smallest distance (smaller sum on
ties). O(n²).

question.md:
Return the sum of three values (different positions) closest to `target`; on a tie, the smaller sum.

- **Up to 1000 values**: O(n³) is about 1.7 × 10⁸ triples, O(n²) is 5 × 10⁵.
- Small values (|v| ≤ 1000), so no overflow worries.

think.md:
Values `[4, -2, 9, 1, -6, 7]`, target 6: the closest sums are [6, 5, 7]…, so **6**.

Same skeleton as 3-sum: fix the smallest value and squeeze the other two. The squeeze doesn't stop early; it
moves toward the target and records the best sum along the way. The skipped pairs are always farther from the
target than one already seen.

idea.md: Check every triple, keeping the best by (distance, sum).

lines.text: Closer wins; equally close, the smaller sum.

limits.md: ~1.7 × 10⁸ triples at n = 1000. Fixing one value and squeezing the other two visits only O(n²) triples without missing the best one.

approaches.title: Sort, fix one, squeeze toward the target

idea.md: Sort. For each `i`, squeeze `j`, `k` over the rest; update the best each time; move `j` up if the sum is below the target, `k` down if above, return immediately on an exact hit.

lines.text: Sort a copy; any triple is a starting answer.
Fix the smallest of the three.
Closer wins; equally close, the smaller sum.
Move toward the target; an exact hit can't be beaten.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²).** **Space O(n)** for the sorted copy.

walk.title: Sort, fix the smallest value, squeeze the other two toward the target, and remember the closest sum seen.

takeaways.md:
- **Closest 3-sum:** the 3-sum skeleton, recording the best instead of stopping at a match.
- Moving toward the target never skips a closer sum (same argument as 2-sum).
- Spell out the tie rule in code: `(distance, sum)` comparisons do it neatly.
